subject: Science
source: Based on the uploaded Class 6 Curiosity Chapter 4 PDF (fecu104.pdf), Reprint 2026–27. Original supplementary material; textbook passages are not reproduced.
goals: Recognise that magnetic effects are strongest near the poles.
Describe attraction and repulsion between poles.
Explain how a freely suspended magnet can help identify directions.
Distinguish magnetic materials from materials that are not attracted to a magnet.
summary: Magnets can attract certain materials, especially iron and some iron-containing materials. Every magnet has two poles, commonly called north and south. Like poles repel and unlike poles attract. The magnetic effect is strongest near the poles. A freely suspended magnet tends to align approximately north–south, which is the principle used by a magnetic compass.

concepts.title: Magnetic and non-magnetic materials
concepts.explanation: A magnet attracts some materials strongly, such as iron and many steels. Materials such as wood, paper, plastic and glass are not attracted in the same ordinary classroom test. Do not assume every metal is magnetic: aluminium and copper are not attracted like iron by a common bar magnet.
concepts.example: Bring a magnet near an iron nail, a wooden stick and an aluminium can. Record which objects are attracted; do not generalise from the word ‘metal’ alone.

concepts.title: Poles of a magnet
concepts.explanation: A magnet has two poles, north and south. The magnetic effect is strongest near the ends of a bar magnet, where iron filings tend to gather more densely. Cutting a magnet does not produce an isolated north pole and south pole; each piece has both poles.
concepts.example: If iron filings collect most strongly near both ends of a bar magnet, those regions are its poles.

concepts.title: Attraction and repulsion
concepts.explanation: When two magnets are brought together, like poles repel and unlike poles attract. Attraction alone does not prove that an object is a magnet, because a magnet can also attract an unmagnetised piece of suitable magnetic material.
concepts.example: North pole facing north pole: repulsion. North pole facing south pole: attraction.

concepts.title: Finding directions
concepts.explanation: A freely suspended magnet turns until it aligns approximately along the north–south direction. A compass places a small magnetised needle on a low-friction pivot so it can turn. Nearby magnets and magnetic objects can disturb the reading.
concepts.example: Place a compass flat and away from magnets, let the needle settle, then use its marked end and the compass directions to orient a map.

concepts.title: Careful magnetic experiments
concepts.explanation: Keep the test conditions consistent and record each object tested. Avoid placing magnets close to electronic devices, magnetic cards or medical devices that could be affected. Follow teacher guidance when using strong magnets.
concepts.example: Use the same magnet and a similar distance for each object, then record attraction as observed rather than assuming from appearance.

workedExamples.question: A magnet attracts a steel paper clip but not a plastic ruler. What conclusion is justified?
steps: Record the direct result: the paper clip is attracted in this test; the ruler is not.
The result supports that the paper clip contains a magnetic material and the ruler does not respond to this magnet in the same way.
Avoid concluding that every metal object will be attracted.
workedExamples.answer: The paper clip is attracted by the magnet, while the plastic ruler is not; material type matters.

workedExamples.question: A compass needle turns when a bar magnet is brought close. Why should the compass be moved away before finding direction?
steps: A compass needle is itself a small magnet.
The nearby bar magnet exerts a magnetic force on the needle.
The needle may then point according to the nearby magnet rather than Earth’s magnetic field.
workedExamples.answer: The nearby magnet disturbs the compass reading, so use it away from magnetic interference.

practice.question: Name the two poles of a magnet.
practice.why: Every ordinary magnet has both poles.

practice.question: What happens when like poles are brought close?
practice.why: Like poles repel; unlike poles attract.

practice.question: Why is ‘all metals are attracted to magnets’ incorrect?
practice.answer: Common magnets strongly attract iron and some iron-containing materials, but metals such as aluminium and copper are not attracted in the same way in a simple classroom test.
practice.why: Magnetic response depends on the material, not simply whether it is called a metal.

practice.question: What is the basic principle of a magnetic compass?
practice.answer: A freely turning magnetised needle aligns approximately north–south.
practice.why: The needle responds to Earth’s magnetic field, unless nearby interference affects it.

mcqs.q: A common bar magnet attracts an iron nail because iron is…
The magnetic effect of a bar magnet is strongest near its…
mcqs.why: The poles are at the regions near the ends where magnetic effects are strongest.
The magnetised needle turns to align with the magnetic field.

mcqs.q: Which is a sensible test procedure?
options: Change the magnet every time without recording it
Test objects consistently and record the result
Assume every metal behaves the same
mcqs.why: Consistent testing and records make comparisons more reliable.

revision: Magnets attract some materials, especially iron and certain iron-containing materials.
Every ordinary magnet has north and south poles; magnetic effects are strongest near the poles.
Like poles repel; unlike poles attract.
A freely suspended magnet aligns approximately north–south, forming the basis of a compass.
Nearby magnets and magnetic materials can disturb compass readings.

chapterTest.instructions: Use the rules of poles and explain each conclusion from the observed evidence.

questions.q: Describe the result when north and south poles are brought close, and when two north poles are brought close.
questions.answer: North and south attract; two north poles repel.

questions.q: Why can’t attraction alone prove that an object is a magnet?
questions.answer: A magnet can attract an unmagnetised piece of magnetic material as well as another magnet. Repulsion between known poles is a clearer test of pole interaction.

questions.q: Explain how a compass helps a traveller find directions and name one source of error.
questions.answer: Its freely turning magnetised needle aligns approximately north–south. Nearby magnets or magnetic objects can disturb the direction.

questions.q: A magnet attracts an iron pin but not a wooden pencil. What does this show?
questions.answer: The materials respond differently to the magnet; iron is magnetic in this test and wood is not attracted.
